Intr oduction
Furan-2(5H)-ones represent a prominent class of
structural scaff olds widely found in natural products
and biologically active compounds (Figure 1).
[1]
Alle-
noic acids have been intensively employed as synthons
to obtain furan-2(5H)-one derivatives, owing to their
high reactivity and easy preparation.
[2]
For example,
Ma and co-workers initially developed palladium-
catalyzed coupling cyclization of 2,3-allenoic acids
with allenes,
[3]
alkynes,
[4]
alkenes,
[5]
or aryl iodides
[6]
to
aff ord polysubstituted butenolides (Scheme 1a). After-
ward, Ma
[7]
and Qing
[8]
reported the copper -catalyzed
free radical cyclization of 2,3-allenoic acids with
various free radical donors to form various furan-
2(5H)-one compounds. In addition, W u
[9]
and co-
workers reported the synthesis of arylsulfonylated
butenolides via a copper(II)-catalyzed three-component
reaction (Scheme 1b). Despite the successful imple-
mentation of these synthetic methods, the development
of novel types of catalysts and multicomponent
reactions to obtain complex furan-2(5H)-ones remains
highly desirable.
Cyanoalkylsulfonyl groups are valuable or ganic
building blocks for the synthesis of bioactive
molecules.
[10]
In addition, they can also be easily
transformed into other useful functional groups.
[1 1]
In
recent years, various synthetic approaches have been
established for the introduction of cyanoalkylsulfonyl
groups. In 2008, Felton
[12]
reported the electrochemical
reduction of alkyl vinyl sulfones with acetonitrile to
obtain cyanoalkylsulfonyl groups. Later , Landais and
coworkers
[13]
demonstrated the three-component cya-
noalkylsulfonylation of α-bromosulfone, olefin, and p-
tosyl cyanide. Moreover , Chen
[14]
reported the copper-
catalyzed cross-coupling of oxime esters and sulfinates
for the synthesis of cyanoalkylsulfonyl groups.

In addition, changing the reaction temperature and
reducing the reaction time resulted in lower yields

Based on the above optimized conditions, we next
explored the substrate cyanoalkylsulfonylation reaction
with dif ferent allenes (Scheme 2). W e mainly consid-
ered 2,3-allenoic acids bearing the R
1
substituent group
on the aromatic ring. Diff erent substituents containing
electron-donating groups such as methyl and methoxy
groups in para position or bis-methyl substituents of
the aromatic ring reacted smoothly and with high
eff iciency , delivering the cyclization products 3 a–3 d
in 67–78% yields. Halogen substituents at the para,
ortho, or meta positions of the aromatic ring were also
well tolerated, affor ding the corresponding compounds
3 e–3 i in 22–59% yields. However , substrate 1, bearing
methyl and methoxy groups at the ortho position,
delivered the desired products 3 j and 3 k in relatively
low yields compared to electron-donating groups at the
para position, presumably due to steric hindrance
eff ects. In addition, when the aromatic ring was
replaced by a naphthalene unit, an unexpected cycliza-
tion product (3 l) was formed in 70% yield. Interest-
ingly , this reaction type could also be utilized for the
substrate with n-propyl as R
3

T o further extend the versatility of this radical
cascade cyclization reaction, we evaluated a series of
3-substituted cyclobutanone oxime esters 2
(Scheme 3). As expected, various functional groups
including aryl, benzyl, ester , and benzyloxy moieties
were compatible, producing the desired products 4 a–
4 k (25–60%). Importantly , 3-disubstituted compounds
also reacted smoothly to aff ord the 4 l and 4 m
compounds in 51% and 19% yields. However , other
cycloketone oximes 2 n and 2 o failed to form the
desired product.
W e synthesized derivatives of sulfonylated product
3 a, to demonstrate its synthetic value (Scheme 4). For
instance, 3 a could undergo lactone ring opening and
butanolysis to yield product 5 a in the presence of n-
butanol and ZnCl
2
. Furthermore, the cyano group of
3 a can easily be transformed to provide the N-tert-
butyl-substituted amide 5 b through a Ritter reaction.
A series of control experiments were conducted to
determine the detailed reaction mechanism (Scheme 5).
Although product 3 a was not obtained in the presence
of the 1,1-diphenylethene (DPE), TEMPO, and BHT
radical scavengers, compound 6 was detected by GC-
MS. Furthermore, compounds 7 and 8 could be
isolated in 34% and 13% yield respectively when DPE
was added to a sulfonylation reaction mixture. These
experimental results indicate the occurrence of a
radical process in this reaction. On the other hand, no
reaction occurred when the 2,3-allenoate 9 replaced
allenoic acid, proving the crucial role of allenoic acid
as a directing group for the cyanoalkylsulfonylation

Based on the control experiments discussed above
as well as previous studies,
[7,8,15a–c]
we propose a
possible free radical pathway for the present cascade
cyclization. (Scheme 6). Initially , SET reduction of the
cycloketone oxime ester 2 a catalyzed by Fe(II) leads
to the cleavage of N � O bonds, forming the iminyl
radical intermediate A. Subsequently , the C � C bond
cleavage of intermediate A yields the alkyl radical
species B. Next, sulfur dioxide, originated from
K
2
S
2
O
5
, attacks the intermediate B to give sulfonyl
radical C, followed by addition to 2,3-allenoic acid 1 a
to form the intermediate D. Under Fe(III) catalysis, the
allylic cation E is generated from the oxidation of
radical species D, while Fe(II) is regenerated. Finally ,
the intramolecular nucleophilic attack of intermediate
D yields the cyclization product 3 a.
Conclusion
In conclusion, we have successfully developed an iron-
catalyzed cyanoalkylsulfonylation of 2,3-allenoic
acids, leading to a variety of cyanoalkylsulfonylated
butenolides under mild conditions. The use of K
2
S
2
O
5
as sulfur dioxide surrogate renders this approach both
safer and more environmentally friendly than other
synthetic methods. Moreover , further transformations
of the cyanoalkylsulfonylated butenolides provided the
corresponding derivatives. Most of these compounds
were previously unknown; additional experiments
evaluating the further applicability of this protocol are
currently being performed in our laboratory .
